analysis.investment_thesis: India Shelter Finance is a financial company — explicitly excluded from the Magic Formula because borrowed capital IS the product, making EBIT/EV and ROIC meaningless as screens. On available proxies, earnings yield of ~5.4% (P/E 18.4×) and ROCE of 12.6% both fall well short of my dual-threshold requirements.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 38.5% (2021–2025) with net profit CAGR of 44.4% — genuine operational momentum
Operating margins expanding to 42.3% (EBITDA 424 Cr on revenue 1,166 Cr in FY25)
Solid DII + FII institutional ownership (28.2% combined) signals credibility in capital markets
key_risks: Earnings yield of only ~5.4% (P/E 18.4×, forward 14.3×) — well below Magic Formula's 12% floor
ROCE of 12.6% and ROE of 15.1% are both below the 20%+ threshold I require for a 'good business'
Debt/Equity at 1.88× and negative FCF every single year (-1,443 Cr in FY25) — capital is continuously consumed, not generated
red_flags: Financial company: Magic Formula explicitly excludes HFCs/NBFCs — debt is raw material, not a risk metric
0 of 5 years with positive operating cash flow — structurally cash-consumptive model
Finance costs growing at 35.4% CAGR, nearly matching revenue growth — spread compression risk
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula begins with a hard rule: exclude financial companies and utilities. India Shelter Finance is a housing finance company where borrowings fund loans — that's the business model. Applying EBIT/EV here is like measuring a bank's 'return on capital' excluding deposits. It doesn't work. The magic formula gives no signal here, and forcing it produces misleading results. Earnings yield using net profit/market cap comes to ~4.3% (378 Cr / 8,738 Cr), and if I use operating income as a proxy for EBIT and add debt to get EV (~13,525 Cr), the yield falls to ~3.6% — far below the 12% minimum I care about.

Setting aside the exclusion issue, the underlying business metrics are mediocre by Magic Formula standards. ROCE of 12.6% and ROE of 15.1% are below my 20% threshold for a 'good' business. The 38.5% revenue CAGR is impressive, but it's driven by growing a loan book funded by external debt — there's no capital-light engine here. The P/B of 2.98× and P/S of 8.9× suggest the market is pricing in continued strong growth, leaving little margin of safety. Even if I admired this business, I'd need to see earnings yield above 12% and ROIC above 20% to act — neither condition is met.
